newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU to extend safeguards against rice imports.
newsitem.headline: EU to extend safeguards against rice imports.

text.p: The European Union is due on Monday to extend safeguard measures against duty free rice imports from member states' overseas territories, setting a tariff quota of 69,610 tonnes from May 1 to November 30, 1997.

The British territories of Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands will be allocated 13,450 tonnes with the remaining 56,160 tonnes for rice coming from other overseas countries and territories (OCT), mostly from the Dutch Antilles.
Following a sharp increase in rice imports from the OCTs, the EU imposed a limit of 44,278 tonnes from January to April.
The European Commission in April recommended extension of the safeguard measures for several more months in order to prevent serious disturbance in the oversaturated EU rice market.

In 1991 the EU agreed that rice produced in former European colonies in Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific (ACP states) could enjoy the duty free access granted to imports from the EU's overseas territories after a small amount of processing.
Rice imported directly from the ACPs benefits only from a 50 percent cut in customs duty within a yearly 125,000-tonne quota.
As a result of the 1991 trade agreement with the overseas territories, imports of OCT rice shot up from 58,000 tonnes in 1992 to an estimated 365,029 tonnes in 1996.
The surge is mostly in rice processed in the Dutch Antilles.
Some of the rice comes from the ACP states of Guyana and Surinam but the Commission also suspects rice from the United States is being illegally brought into the EU via the OCT route.
"We have a strong suspicion it is U.S. rice," Commission spokesman Joao Vale de Almeida told Reuters.

Next Monday's meeting of EU foreign ministers is also due to rekindle a simmering row between the Netherlands and the other 14 EU member states, who are backed by the Commission in demanding changes to the 1991 OCT agreement.

The Netherlands, which currently holds the EU presidency, has consistently blocked attempts to set upper annual limits on the duty free imports from the OCTs of sensitive products including rice and sugar, and no progress is expected on Monday.

"We are against the current situation. It is pure commercial speculation which doesn't benefit either the ACPs or the overseas territories. It benefits a handful of operators who have found a loophole and damages Community and ACP production," spokesman Vale de Almeida said.
Frustration with the lack of progress on the OCT agreement and disturbances to the EU market led rice-producers Italy and Spain to demand safeguard measures last December.
The new May-November safeguard limit is based on annual average imports of 163,000 tonnes between 1992 and 1995.
